Title: Copycat Takeout Fried Rice — The Cold Rice Secret
Description: Why is takeout fried rice never mushy? Cold, day-old rice. It's drier on the outside, so the grains fry and toast instead of sticking. Title: How to Brown Butter — The Easy Restaurant Flavor Secret
Description: Brown butter is a restaurant trick for deep, nutty flavor. Melt butter in a light-colored pan over medium heat, swirl it as it foams, and watch: when the little bits at the bottom turn golden brown and it smells like toasted nuts, take it off the heat. Title: Should You Rinse Pasta? Why Italian Cooks Don't
Description: Don't rinse cooked pasta for a hot dish. The thin layer of starch on the outside is what helps sauce cling, and rinsing washes it away and cools the pasta. Drain it, save a mug of the cooking water, and toss the pasta straight into the warm sauce with a splash of that water. The one exception: some cold pasta salads. Description: Happy hour isn't only about drinks. Many restaurants have a bar or early-evening menu with smaller plates and appetizers at lower prices, from the same kitchen. Title: Which Pasta Shape for Which Sauce? The Easy Italian Rule
Description: Italian cooks pick the pasta shape for the sauce. Chunky meat or vegetable sauces go with tubes and ridged shapes like rigatoni and penne that catch the bits. Smooth, creamy or oily sauces suit long strands like spaghetti, linguine and fettuccine. Small shapes like ditalini go in soup. Wide flat noodles love rich sauces. Title: How Restaurants Make Mashed Potatoes So Creamy
Description: The restaurant way to creamy mashed potatoes for Thanksgiving: start the potatoes in cold, salted water so they cook evenly, drain and let them steam dry in the pot, warm the butter and milk, and mash gently with a ricer or masher, never a blender. Title: How to Spot Real Parmigiano Reggiano at the Store
Description: Parmigiano Reggiano is a protected cheese from a specific area of northern Italy, and its rind is stamped with the name in a pattern of little dots. Cheese sold as just "parmesan" can be made anywhere and in different ways. Neither is bad, but read the label and the rind so you know what you're buying. Buy a wedge and grate it yourself. Description: "Kids eat free" nights can save a family real money, but read the rules first. Title: The Restaurant Trick for Food That Tastes Flat — Add Acid
Description: Your soup, stew or sauce tastes fine but flat? Restaurant cooks often finish dishes with a little acid: a squeeze of lemon, a splash of red wine vinegar or balsamic, a spoon of tomato. It brightens all the other flavors. Add a little at the end, stir and taste, before reaching for more salt. Works on bean soups, chili, roasted vegetables and pan sauces. Title: Whole vs Crushed Canned Tomatoes — The Italian Sauce Trick
Description: Many Italian cooks buy whole peeled canned tomatoes and crush them by hand or with a spoon. Whole tomatoes are often the better-quality fruit in the can, and crushing them yourself gives a fresher, chunkier sauce. Read the label for just tomatoes, juice and salt, taste one straight from the can, and simmer gently. Sunday sauce tips from Chef Sal Romano. More on Sal's page.

Title: "Still or Sparkling?" — The Restaurant Water Question
Description: At some restaurants, the first question is "still or sparkling?" Answer either one and you may get a bottle of water that shows up on the bill. If you'd like regular tap water, it's perfectly normal to say "tap water is fine, thanks." If you want bottled, ask the price. Small habits like this keep a dinner out from creeping up. Title: What to Do With Stale Bread — The Italian Way
Description: Italian home cooking wastes nothing, and stale bread is an ingredient. Blitz it into breadcrumbs for meatballs and toppings, toast cubes in olive oil for croutons, toss it with tomatoes and onion for panzanella, or simmer it into a thick Tuscan-style bean soup. Title: How to Buy Better Olive Oil — Check the Harvest Date
Description: Olive oil tastes best fresh. At the store, look for a harvest date (not just a best-by date), a dark glass bottle or tin that blocks light, and "extra virgin" for drizzling and finishing. Title: How to Roast Vegetables So They Get Crispy, Not Soggy
Description: Restaurant roasted vegetables are browned and crispy because they aren't crowded. Spread them in a single layer with space between pieces, use two sheet pans if you need to, preheat the oven, toss with enough oil and salt, and don't stir too often. Title: Sharing an Entree at a Restaurant — Ask About the Split Fee
Description: Restaurant portions are often big enough for two. Sharing an entree is a smart way to eat out for less, but some places add a split-plate charge or an extra side fee. Title: Holiday Leftovers — The 2-Hour Rule and How Long They Keep
Description: After Thanksgiving dinner, pack up the leftovers before the pie. USDA food safety guidance says to refrigerate cooked food within 2 hours, use it within 3 to 4 days, or freeze it. Title: Why Baking Recipes Say Room-Temperature Butter and Eggs
Description: Most cake and cookie recipes call for room-temperature butter and eggs for a reason. Soft butter creams with sugar and traps tiny air bubbles that help baked goods rise, and room-temperature eggs blend in smoothly instead of curdling the batter. Take them out ahead of time, or set whole eggs in warm water for a few minutes. Holiday baking tips from Chef Sal Romano.

Title: Restaurant-Style Garlic Bread — The Broiler Trick
Description: For restaurant-style garlic bread, mix soft butter with fresh minced garlic, a little grated parmesan and parsley, spread it on split Italian bread and bake until warm, then finish under the broiler until golden.
